title: Only the bird's head
hookLine: book three opens with the three inner limbs in three short sutras: hold the mind in one place, let it flow, then disappear into what you're seeing
carry: dharana, dhyana, samadhi: hold, flow, only the target

lines: A WOODEN BIRD IN A TREE.
cards: The teacher Drona sets a wooden bird high in a tree and calls his students to aim. In a story often told from the Mahabharata, he asks each one before he shoots: what do you see?
One sees the tree, the branches, the sky, his brothers. Drona sends him away. Then Arjuna steps up.
What do you see? The bird. Describe the bird.
I see only its head. Shoot. Popular retellings make it the eye; the epic says the head.

teach.h: DHARANA: HOLD THE MIND IN ONE PLACE.
teach.b: Sutra 3.1: dharana, concentration, is binding the mind to one place.
The classical commentary lists places: the navel, the lotus of the heart, the light in the head, the tip of the nose, the tip of the tongue, or something outside the body.
Dharana comes from a root meaning to hold, the same root as dharma. You hold the mind there, the way you'd hold a cup steady. It slips.
You bring it back. That's dharana.

Sutra 3.2: dhyana, meditation, is when the idea of that object flows on without a break. One thread, no knots. A later image some teachers use: oil poured from one jar to another, a single unbroken stream.

Sutra 3.3: samadhi, absorption, is that same flow when only the object shines, as if empty of its own form. In dhyana, there's still you, meditating on something. In samadhi, the sense of me meditating drops away.
Only the bird's head. Arjuna in the story isn't thinking, I'm concentrating well. There's just the target.
These aren't three separate techniques. They're one movement, deepening. Hold.
Flow. Disappear into it. Hindu worship trains this every day.

teach.h: A VERSE THAT PAINTS THE GOD'S FORM.
teach.b: Before many pujas, families recite a dhyana shloka, a meditation verse that paints the god's form. One well-loved verse pictures a god clad in white, bright as the moon, with four arms; many families say it for Ganesha.
The verse gives the mind one bird's head to hold. Patanjali's claim is that this can be trained, and pointed at the deepest things.

how: In Hindu worship and meditation, practitioners often fix attention on one point, such as a sacred image, a mantra or the heart, and many begin puja with a dhyana shloka, a verse describing the deity's form; teachers describe concentration deepening into meditation and absorption over long practice.

games.q: nani recites a verse describing ganesha's form before she starts puja. by sutra 3.1, what is the verse doing?
o: telling ganesha what he looks like.
giving her mind one place to hold: dharana.
filling time until the lamp is lit.
games.why: 3.1: dharana is binding the mind to one place. a dhyana shloka gives the mind one form to hold, the way arjuna saw only the bird's head; held long enough, it flows (3.2) and deepens (3.3).

practice: Choose one place, the tip of the nose where the breath touches or the center of the chest, and hold the mind there; when it slips, and it will, bring it back without scolding. That's dharana.
If for a few breaths it stays without your holding, notice the flow: a taste of dhyana.

wordCard.voice: Concentration. Dharana, binding the mind to one place, the first of the three inner limbs, which deepen into meditation and absorption.

orig.note: Sanskrit dhyāna: meditation, the unbroken flow of attention; the seventh limb, between dhāraṇā and samādhi.

carryVoice: Your line: dharana, dhyana, samadhi: hold, flow, only the target. Book three opens with seeing only the bird's head. Rest well.
